title: psql Essentials: Finding Your Way Around a Database
intro: Sooner or later an incident ends at a database prompt. psql is PostgreSQL's command-line client, and its backslash commands are how you find out what's in a database you've never seen. The database is shop, on host db.internal, and your user is app.

steps.prompt: Connect to the database shop on host db.internal as user app.
steps.fake_output:
Password for user app:
psql (16.4)
SSL connection (protocol: TLSv1.3, cipher: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384)
Type "help" for help.

shop=>
steps.explanation: You're connected, over TLS. The prompt shows the database name.
steps.why: The prompt's last character matters: '=>' is an ordinary user and '=#' is a superuser. Check it before running anything destructive. For scripts, put the password in ~/.pgpass or the PGPASSWORD variable, never on the command line where it shows up in the process list and shell history.

steps.prompt: You're inside psql. Confirm exactly which server, port, database, and user this session is connected to.
steps.fake_output:
You are connected to database "shop" as user "app" on host "db.internal" (address "10.0.2.15") at port "5432".
SSL connection (protocol: TLSv1.3)
steps.why: The most expensive database mistakes are the right command on the wrong server. With several terminals open during an incident, \conninfo before a write costs two seconds. Many teams also colour the production prompt red in .psqlrc for the same reason.

steps.prompt: List the tables in this database.
steps.fake_output:
List of relations
 Schema |    Name     | Type  | Owner
--------+-------------+-------+-------
 public | customers   | table | shop
 public | order_items | table | shop
 public | orders      | table | shop
 public | products    | table | shop
steps.explanation: Four tables, all in the public schema.
steps.why: Backslash commands are psql's own, not SQL: \dt tables, \l databases, \dn schemas, \du roles, \di indexes. Add + for sizes (\dt+). They're shortcuts for queries on the system catalogs; 'psql -E' shows the SQL behind each one.

steps.prompt: Show the structure of the orders table: columns, indexes, and constraints.
steps.fake_output:
Table "public.orders"
   Column    |           Type           | Nullable |      Default
-------------+--------------------------+----------+-------------------
 id          | bigint                   | not null | generated always
 customer_id | bigint                   | not null |
 status      | text                     | not null | 'pending'::text
 total_cents | integer                  | not null |
 created_at  | timestamp with time zone | not null | now()
Indexes:
    "orders_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (id)
    "idx_orders_customer_created" btree (customer_id, created_at DESC)
Foreign-key constraints:
    "orders_customer_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
Referenced by:
    TABLE "order_items" CONSTRAINT "order_items_order_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id)
steps.explanation: Five columns, two indexes, and foreign keys in both directions.
steps.why: \d is the first thing to run on any table in a slow-query investigation: it shows which indexes exist, so you can tell whether a query could use one. The 'Referenced by' section tells you what a DELETE here would be checked against.

steps.prompt: Wide rows are unreadable in a table. Switch to expanded output, which prints one column per line.
steps.why: Views like pg_stat_activity have 20 or more columns and wrap badly. '\x auto' switches only when a row is too wide for the terminal, and is worth putting in ~/.psqlrc. '\timing' is the other toggle to know: it prints how long each statement took.

steps.prompt: Leave psql. From the shell, run one statement non-interactively: count the rows in orders. Print only the bare value, with no headers or alignment.
expected_commands: psql -h db.internal -U app -d shop -At -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders"
psql -h db.internal -U app -d shop -At -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
psql -h db.internal -U app -d shop -A -t -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders"
psql -h db.internal -U app -d shop -A -t -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
steps.hint: -c runs one statement; -A turns off alignment and -t prints tuples only.
steps.explanation: Just the number, ready for a script to use.
steps.why: -c runs one statement and exits, and -At strips the decoration, which is what monitoring checks and shell scripts need. To run a file safely use 'psql -f file.sql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -1': stop at the first error, and wrap the whole file in one transaction, so a failure half-way leaves nothing behind.
